title: Grade 11 Physics — Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
description: Rotational motion — centre of mass, torque, moment of inertia, angular momentum, rolling motion (CBSE Ch. 7)
subject: physics

questions.question: The centre of mass of a system of two equal masses m separated by distance d is:
questions.explanation: For two equal masses m at positions x₁ and x₂: x_cm = (m·x₁ + m·x₂)/(2m) = (x₁ + x₂)/2 — the midpoint. The centre of mass lies at the midpoint when masses are equal.

questions.question: Torque (τ) is defined as:
questions.explanation: Torque τ = r × F = rF sinθ, where r is the position vector and θ is the angle between r and F. It is the rotational analogue of force — the tendency to cause rotation. SI unit: N·m.

questions.question: Moment of inertia depends on:
options: Mass and its distribution about the axis
questions.explanation: Moment of inertia I = Σmᵢrᵢ² depends on both the total mass and how that mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation. A hollow cylinder has a larger I than a solid cylinder of the same mass and radius.

questions.question: The moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere of mass M and radius R about a diameter is:
questions.explanation: I = (2/5)MR² for a solid sphere about a diameter. Compare: hollow sphere = (2/3)MR²; solid disk about central axis = ½MR²; thin ring = MR².

questions.question: The theorem of parallel axes states: I = I_cm + ___
questions.explanation: Parallel axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md², where I_cm is the moment of inertia about the axis through the centre of mass, M is the total mass, and d is the distance between the two parallel axes.

questions.question: Angular momentum L of a rigid body rotating with angular velocity ω is:
questions.explanation: L = Iω, where I is the moment of inertia. This is the rotational analogue of linear momentum p = mv. SI unit: kg·m²/s.

questions.question: A diver tucks in her arms and legs during a flip. Her angular velocity:
questions.explanation: By conservation of angular momentum (no external torque): L = Iω = constant. Tucking in reduces I (mass closer to axis). To keep L constant, ω must increase.

questions.question: The rotational kinetic energy of a body with moment of inertia I rotating at ω is:
questions.explanation: Rotational KE = ½Iω². This is the rotational analogue of translational KE = ½mv². For rolling motion, total KE = ½mv² + ½Iω².

questions.question: Newton's second law for rotation states:
questions.explanation: τ_net = Iα, where τ is net torque, I is moment of inertia, and α is angular acceleration. This is the rotational analogue of F = ma.

questions.question: For a rolling object (without slipping), the relationship between linear velocity v and angular velocity ω is:
questions.explanation: For rolling without slipping: v = ωR, where R is the radius. The contact point has zero velocity, and the top has velocity 2v. This is the rolling constraint.

questions.question: A wheel of moment of inertia 2 kg·m² is rotating at 5 rad/s. The torque needed to stop it in 10 s is:
questions.explanation: α = (ω_f − ω_i)/t = (0 − 5)/10 = −0.5 rad/s². Torque τ = Iα = 2 × 0.5 = 1 N·m (magnitude).

questions.question: The perpendicular axes theorem applies to:
questions.explanation: Perpendicular axis theorem: for a lamina in the XY-plane, I_z = I_x + I_y. This applies only to flat (2D) bodies (laminas), not to 3D objects.

questions.question: A solid cylinder and a hollow cylinder of the same mass and radius roll down an incline without slipping from rest. Which reaches the bottom first?
questions.explanation: The acceleration of a rolling body on an incline is a = g sinθ/(1 + I/MR²). Solid cylinder: I = ½MR² → a = (2/3)g sinθ. Hollow: I = MR² → a = ½g sinθ. Solid cylinder has greater acceleration and reaches first.

questions.question: The relation between torque τ and angular momentum L is:
questions.explanation: τ = dL/dt — torque is the rate of change of angular momentum. This is directly analogous to F = dp/dt (force = rate of change of linear momentum). When τ = 0, L is conserved.

questions.question: The centre of mass of the Earth-Moon system lies:
options: At the centre of the Earth
At the centre of the Moon
Inside the Earth, closer to its centre
questions.explanation: The Earth is ~81 times more massive than the Moon. The centre of mass = (M_E × 0 + M_M × d)/(M_E + M_M) ≈ d/82 ≈ 4700 km from Earth's centre. Since Earth's radius ≈ 6400 km, the CM is inside the Earth.
